intuition: For one value from the first sorted array, pairing it with the second array gives a sorted row of sums. Treat these rows as sorted lists. Keep each row's next pair in a heap, take the smallest pair, then advance only that row.

Think of a matrix whose row i contains nums1[i]+nums2[j] across all columns. Each row is already sorted, and its first unreturned entry is its only candidate for the next globally smallest pair. A min-heap compares those row fronts. After emitting one, advance only that row. Pair indices remain separate even when values repeat, preserving occurrence count.
At most k starting rows are relevant: their first entries already supply k sums no larger than the first entry of any later row.

The heap holds the smallest unreturned pair in every seeded row, so its minimum is the next globally smallest pair among those rows. Unseeded rows begin no earlier than the kth row; the k seeded row starts already provide k sums no greater than any unseeded start. Thus omitting those rows cannot invalidate the first k sums.
Heap size is at most the number of seeded rows; each emitted pair causes at most one insertion.

For nums1=[0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7], nums2=[10], and k=2, only row starts with sums 10 and 11 are seeded. Every omitted row begins with sum at least 12, so neither can displace a requested pair. This asymmetric case makes the k-row cap useful even though there are many potential rows.

steps: Pop sum 3 and emit [1,2]; replace that row front with [1,4], sum 5.
Pop sum 5 and emit [1,4]; replace it with [1,6], sum 7.
Pop sum 7 and emit [1,6]; the first row now has no successor.
Three requested pairs are complete, so return [[1,2],[1,4],[1,6]].

codeNotes.note: The heap compares the current smallest unreturned candidate from each seeded sorted row.
Preserve row and column positions so duplicate values still correspond to distinct available pairs.
Only the popped row advances; adding arbitrary neighboring rows again would duplicate pair positions.

keyDecision: After taking pair (i, j), add (i, j + 1) if that column exists.

concept.question: Why is each first-array value the head of an ordered row of pairs?
intuition: Forming all pairs wastes work when only a few smallest sums are requested. With sorted arrays, pairing one fixed first value with successive second values creates an ascending row of sums.
Keep only the next unseen pair from each relevant row. Select the smallest row head, output it, and advance that row by one. The row heads collectively represent the smallest pair not yet returned.
concept.observation: After removing a row head, expose only the next pair in that same row.
approach: Start a row at the first second-array value for the first few first-array values.
Compare the exposed row heads by pair sum.
Output the smallest head and advance its row until enough pairs are returned.
concept.correctness: Each row is sorted, so its head is its smallest unreturned pair. The minimum among all exposed heads is consequently the global smallest unreturned pair. Advancing only that row restores the invariant. Rows beyond the first requested-count first values cannot be needed earlier, since that many initial row heads already have sums no larger than their first head.

complexity.space: O(min(m, k)) auxiliary plus O(k) output
complexity.explanation: The frontier contains at most the smaller of first-array length and requested count. Each returned pair uses a logarithmic frontier update; extra frontier storage matches that bound, in addition to the output.

scenes.narration: For [1,7,11] and [2,4,6], the initial pairs are (1,2), (7,2), (11,2), with sums 3,9,13. Three results are requested.
scenes.decision: Later pairs in a row cannot precede its current head.

scenes.title: Advance the winning row
scenes.narration: Output (1,2), then expose (1,4), whose sum 5 is still below the other heads 9 and 13. Output it next.
scenes.decision: Every row’s earlier pair has already been removed.

scenes.title: The same row wins once more
scenes.narration: Expose (1,6), sum 7, and select it ahead of 9 and 13. Return [(1,2),(1,4),(1,6)].
scenes.decision: A row may supply several consecutive winners; there is no round-robin rule.
